name: Planning for Inspections and Re-Inspections in Los Angeles Commercial Projects

mainEntity.name: What are common pitfalls when budgeting timelines for inspections, corrections, and re-inspections on Los Angeles County commercial projects?
mainEntity.text: What are common pitfalls when budgeting timelines for inspections, corrections, and re-inspections on Los Angeles County commercial projects?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owners and contractors frequently underestimate how much inspections and corrections affect commercial construction schedules in Los Angeles County. One common pitfall is assuming next-day inspection availability for every trade and stage of work. In practice, inspector workloads, holidays, and high-demand periods can push inspections out by several days. Another issue is failing to plan for correction cycles. If an inspection fails due to incomplete work, unclear details, or missing documentation, additional work and a re-inspection are required, adding delay. Critical activities—such as foundation pours, major concrete placements, or concealed framing and MEP work—cannot proceed until inspectors sign off. Coordinating inspection requests across multiple trades can also be challenging. For example, framing, electrical rough-in, plumbing rough-in, and mechanical rough-in often need to be inspected in a coordinated sequence before closing walls. Misalignment among subcontractors can cause repeated rescheduling. To mitigate these risks, project schedules should include explicit inspection milestones, reasonable float for corrections, and contingency around critical inspections. Clear communication with inspectors, providing complete approved plans on-site, and ensuring work is truly ready before calling for inspection all help reduce rejections. Pre-construction meetings that review inspection expectations can further improve outcomes.
acceptedAnswer.description: Inspection timelines for commercial construction in Los Angeles County are often underestimated. Common pitfalls include assuming next-day inspections, ignoring correction and re-inspection cycles, and failing to coordinate inspector availability with critical pours or closures. Building realistic inspection float into the schedule reduces risk of delays.
